idiom_name: GRDB Codable record written through a serial DispatchQueue
implementation_notes: GRDB turns the stored record into a Codable struct conforming to FetchableRecord/PersistableRecord and the store into a DatabaseQueue (or DatabasePool for concurrent readers): the append is try dbQueue.write { try record.insert(db) }, prepared statements and transactions come with it, and WAL is selected in the configuration, so the classic Store structure becomes one type and two methods. The tap is a serial DispatchQueue (or an actor) owning the database queue, and the delivery path only enqueues, so no message ever waits on the file; retention is a scheduled filtered delete (try dbQueue.write { try StoredMessage.filter(Column("recordedAt") < cutoff).deleteAll($0) }) and reporting is a value observation or fetch over the same database. Hand-write a store protocol with a mock backend when the application must be testable without SQLite; otherwise the record type plus the serial queue is the pattern in full.
pitfalls: DatabaseQueue serialises all access, so a long audit query delays the tap; use a DatabasePool (WAL) with read-only readers for reporting, or a second connection.
try? on the write hides the audit gap; count failures so a misconfigured path cannot silently store nothing.
Constructing the record from the raw payload before redaction leaks sensitive data into the store; redaction belongs at the call site that builds StoredMessage.
GRDB migrations are the store's version history: adding a column without a registered migration makes the database fail to open, not merely a query to fail.
